blocks.lead: Type the C++ template five times from memory. Write the linear sieve once and keep it.
Write the bank transfer. Not read about it. Write it, compile it, run it under contention.
blocks.code: void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, int amt);

items: Naive version with one mutex per account, locked in call order. Run two threads doing `transfer(A,B)` and `transfer(B,A)` in a loop. Watch it deadlock. You need to have seen this, not just know about it.
Fix by imposing a total order on lock acquisition — compare addresses or account IDs, always lock the lower first.
Fix again using `std::scoped_lock(m1, m2)`, which does deadlock-free multi-lock acquisition internally.
Add a balance check that must be atomic with the debit. Explain why checking outside the lock is a TOCTOU bug.

blocks.lead: Then be able to answer, out loud:
items: Why is a single global mutex correct but bad? (Serialises everything, no concurrency.)
`lock_guard` vs `unique_lock` vs `scoped_lock` — when each.
Where would a condition variable go if the transfer must wait for sufficient funds? Why the wait must be in a loop, not an `if`. (Spurious wakeups.)
What does RAII buy you here when an exception is thrown mid-transfer?

blocks.lead: Rewrite five of these without conditionals, then verify with `-O2 -S` or on godbolt that the branch is gone:
items: `max(a,b)` and `min(a,b)` without `if`
`abs(x)` using sign-shift: `(x ^ (x>>31)) - (x>>31)`
Conditional swap of two ints on a predicate
Clamp to `[0, 255]`
Count elements greater than a threshold in a loop — replace `if (a[i] > t) cnt++` with `cnt += (a[i] > t)`
Select between two values: `r = c*a + (1-c)*b`, or better, a mask: `mask = -(long long)c; r = (a & mask) | (b & ~mask)`

blocks.lead: Then know why it matters, because that's the follow-up question: pipeline flush on a mispredicted branch costs ~15–20 cycles, and a data-dependent unpredictable branch defeats the predictor. Also know the counter-argument — a well-predicted branch is nearly free, and branchless code always evaluates both sides, so it can be slower. `cmov` versus a predictable branch is the standard example.

probs.t: Ehab and the Expected XOR Problem

blocks.lead: C++, in rough priority. Your Rust background covers ownership intuition; none of the C++-specific mechanics transfer.
items: `vector` vs `list`: contiguity, cache behaviour, iterator invalidation, when `list` ever wins
`vector` growth: amortised doubling, `reserve`, why `push_back` can invalidate everything
Copy constructor vs move constructor vs assignment — when each fires, and what `std::move` actually does (it's a cast)
Virtual dispatch: vtable and vptr layout, cost of an indirect call, why `virtual` in a hot loop is an HFT sin
`unique_ptr` vs `shared_ptr`, and why `shared_ptr` refcounting is atomic and therefore not free
RAII, and why destructors make exception safety work

blocks.lead: Architecture, shallower. These are the ones an HFT firm actually cares about:
items: Cache lines (64 bytes), spatial and temporal locality
False sharing — two threads writing adjacent variables on one line, and the fix (padding, `alignas(64)`)
Row-major vs column-major traversal and why the timing difference is 5–10x
Branch prediction, connecting back to Day 2
Rough latency numbers: L1 ~1ns, L2 ~4ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD ~100µs. Know the orders of magnitude

blocks.lead: OS. You have CS F372, so this is revision, not learning. Prioritise: mutex vs semaphore vs spinlock and when a spinlock is correct; context-switch cost; virtual memory, page tables, TLB; what a page fault costs.
Networks. Lowest priority given three days. TCP vs UDP and why an HFT shop cares about UDP and kernel-bypass. Twenty minutes, no more.

probs.t: Omkar and Last Class of Math
